doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Musicians supporting each other
summary: Showing up unprepared sidemen, and how players of the older era comped to make each other sound good.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: That’s a good story, and it’s very interesting that you showed up for this date and you didn’t know he was on it, right?

And he didn’t know who was the soloist on this date either. The way that thing works is, I think, very interesting. It’s always sort of been that way in jazz. You just are prepared or don’t be in the business.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. And there’s a certain kind of a coming together, hopefully. It’s a supportive thing. Everybody’s supporting each other, especially from that era, to me. Musicians used to play to make each other sound good, as opposed to, “okay it’s my turn to shine.” You know? When somebody was soloing, I mean they would comp to make him sound better. Whoever was playing drums would make it happen. Kick the singer. Kick the tenor player. Whatever. I had somebody tell me one time, doing a gig, and the guitar player didn’t know the bass player and the drummer. And when they arrived in their cars, the bass player and the drummer were riding together. And the guitar player said to me, “nice. I like to see them pull up together.” Because they’re going to play together if they hang together. At least one likes to think so. And it usually does happen that way.
